summary: Describes how to use the Stac LZS data compression algorithm to compress PPP packets using a DCP header. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A recipe for shrinking data on a phone line using one company's squeezing method.

subtitle: Stac LZS compression for PPP links, with a one-byte header that carries reset signals on every packet.

tldr.problem: PPP links can carry more data per second if packets are compressed, but compressors and decompressors that share a running history break badly when a packet is lost, damaged or reordered.
tldr.mechanism: LZS-DCP wraps each Stac LZS compressed datagram in a small DCP header whose bits flag compressed versus uncompressed data and carry Reset-Request and Reset-Ack signals. An optional sequence number and a one-byte check detect lost or damaged packets.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational enhancement of the older Stac LZS option for PPP, written to give a common compression protocol for Stac LZS. The RFC says a pending TIA/EIA-655 standard uses it.

today: RFC 1967 is an Informational RFC and the data shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. The RFC itself says the pending TIA/EIA-655 standard uses this protocol, and that it enhances the older Stac LZS protocol in RFC 1974.

sections.title: Why LZS-DCP Exists
sections.content:
Stac Electronics developed the Stac LZS compression algorithm, which starts from a sliding window compression history similar to LZ1. An earlier PPP protocol for it was published as RFC 1974 (compression type 17). That protocol became the basis for TIA work on DSU/CSUs, which introduced a portable Data Compression Protocol (DCP) header. LZS-DCP combines the two.

The RFC lists three differences from the type 17 protocol. Packets with uncompressible data can be sent without clearing the compression history. Reset request and acknowledgment bits ride in the DCP header of every packet instead of separate CCP packets, which may mean fewer discarded packets during the handshake. Sequence numbers and the check byte can be used together.

The algorithm supports one or several compression histories. One history needs the least memory; several histories, one per virtual connection, can improve the compression ratio.
sections.eli5: Imagine two friends who shorten their notes by pointing back at things they already wrote. This version adds little flags to every note so they can fix mix-ups quickly.

sections.title: How LZS-DCP Packets Are Carried
sections.content:
Before any LZS-DCP packet is sent, PPP MUST reach the Network-Layer Protocol phase and the CCP Control Protocol MUST reach the Opened state. Exactly one LZS-DCP datagram goes in the PPP Information field. The PPP Protocol field is 00FD (compressed datagram) or 00FB (individual link compressed datagram). Type 00FD is used for a single physical link or a single bundle of links; 00FB is used when compression is negotiated separately on individual links to the same destination.

The data being compressed starts with the PPP Protocol ID field, followed by the original Information field. PPP Link Control Protocol packets and Network Control Protocol packets MUST NOT be sent inside LZS-DCP packets. PPP padding is not allowed, though compressed packets can be padded with zeros after the last compressed octet.

The maximum expansion of Stac LZS is 12.5%. If expansion plus the compression header would exceed the peer's MRU, the data MUST be sent as an uncompressed LZS-DCP packet.
sections.eli5: Each squeezed message goes into a labelled envelope. If squeezing would make it bigger, you just send it as it is.

sections.title: The DCP Header and Packet Fields
sections.content:
An LZS-DCP packet is the PPP Protocol field, a one-octet DCP header, an optional history number, an optional sequence number, the data, and an optional Longitudinal Check Byte (LCB). The header bits are E (extension, currently always 1), C/U (1 for compressed data, 0 for uncompressed), R-A (Reset-Ack), R-R (Reset-Request), three reserved bits that MUST be 0, and C/D, which MUST be 0 because CCP already provides negotiation.

The history number is absent when the negotiated History Count is less than 2, one octet for 2 to 255 histories, and two octets for 256 or more. The sequence number is one octet, starts at 1 and increments modulo 256 per history. The LCB is the exclusive-OR of FF hex and every octet of the uncompressed datagram, and appears only on compressed packets.

For compressed packets the data is one block as defined in section 3.2 of ANSI X3.241-1994, with an end marker, and the RFC repeats the block format for information only.
sections.eli5: The header is a row of tiny switches on the envelope: is it squeezed, please start over, okay I started over. A check number lets the receiver notice if the contents got scrambled.

sections.title: Resynchronizing After Errors
sections.content:
A decompressor cannot recover from dropped, erroneous or misordered datagrams and will propagate errors until both peers reset. The sequence number detects dropped or misordered packets and the LCB detects damaged ones. A mismatch is a receive failure for that history.

On a receive failure the receiver MUST send a packet with the R-R bit set, naming the failed history, and MUST discard data for that history until a Reset-Ack arrives. The transmitter MUST clear that history on a Reset-Request and send a packet with R-A set and data in it. It also sets R-A on any packet sent when its history buffer was clear. The receiver is responsible for making the exchange reliable, which may mean asking more than once.

When no history is kept, the algorithm needs neither a reliable link nor in-order delivery, though per-packet compression gives a lower ratio. With histories, an implementation MUST rely on a reliable lower layer, on synchronization, or both.
sections.eli5: If a page goes missing, the reader waves a flag saying start over. The writer starts fresh and waves a flag back, and they carry on from there.

sections.title: The Configuration Option
sections.content:
The LZS-DCP Configuration Option is used in CCP. It has Type 23, Length 6, a two-octet History Count, a Check Mode and a Process Mode. If peers cannot agree, no compression is used.

History Count 0 means the peer must clear the history at the start of every packet; 1 is the default (one history); 2 to 65535 allow several. Check Mode is 0 None, 1 LCB, 2 Sequence Number, or 3 Sequence Number plus LCB (the default); None MUST NOT be used with history counts above zero. Process Mode 0 (None, default) means uncompressed packets do not update the history; 1 (Process-Uncompressed) means both sides add them to their histories, which is how an uncompressed packet can be sent without losing the history.
sections.eli5: Before they start, the two ends agree on the settings, like how many notebooks to keep and how to check for mistakes. If they cannot agree, they skip squeezing.
